deep.reconstruction:
Context (previous page): an n-tuple (y_1,...,y_n) is a 'system' of multivalued functions with branch points a,b,...,g. A closed circuit of x around a branch point transforms the tuple by a constant matrix (A),(B),...,(G). Riemann has shown that systems of the same 'class' (same substitutions) are linearly related with rational coefficients. In particular every system Y of the class can be written through y, y',...,y^(n-1). He now asks how far a system is determined by its 'characteristic', meaning its substitutions plus its exponents at the branch points.

Step 1. Let Y be any system with the same substitutions and the same exponents as y. By the corollary there are polynomials c_0, b_0,...,b_{n-1} in x with
  c_0 Y_i = b_0 y_i + b_1 y_i' + ... + b_{n-1} y_i^(n-1),  i = 1..n.
[My filling-in:] By Cramer's rule, b_j/c_0 = W_j(Y,y)/W(y). Here W(y) is the Wronskian det(y_i^(k)), and W_j is W with column j replaced by Y. Under a circuit, numerator and denominator are both multiplied by det(A). The quotient is therefore single-valued, and given its finite local behaviour it is rational. The denominator c_0 can be taken from W(y) alone: it is the polynomial carrying the extra zeros and the branch-point behaviour of W(y). Hence 'c_0 depends only on the y'. The exponent conditions, including those at infinity, bound the degrees of the b_j. So only finitely many unknown coefficients occur.

Step 2 (converse). For a given choice of b_j, the Y defined by these formulas automatically has the right substitutions. It has the required characteristic exactly when two conditions hold:
- at every branch point its exponents are not lower than those of y;
- at every other finite x (zeros of c_0) it stays finite.
Vanishing of the offending Laurent/Puiseux coefficients is linear and homogeneous in the coefficients of the b_j. (Riemann writes 'b_1,...,b_n'; it should be b_0,...,b_{n-1}.)

Step 3. Solve the linear system.
- If its rank fixes the ratios of the unknowns, the solution space is one-dimensional. Since Y = y is always a solution, the general Y is const·(y).
- Otherwise the general solution is Y = k y + k_1 y^(1) + ... + k_m y^(m). Here y^(1),...,y^(m) are further linearly independent particular systems of the same characteristic, not derivatives: derivatives would lower the exponents. The constants k, k_1,...,k_m are arbitrary.

Step 4 (begins here, finished on the next page). Fix the free constants one after another as functions of the rest. Each time, make the leading coefficient in the expansion of one of the canonical branches (A)^{-1}(Y), (B)^{-1}(Y), ...,(G)^{-1}(Y) at its branch point vanish. Each step raises the exponent sum by at least 1 and removes one free constant. The end result is a system of higher exponents determined by its characteristic up to a common constant factor.

In modern terms: the space of solutions of a Fuchsian system with given monodromy and lower bounds on local exponents is a finite-dimensional vector space. It is computed by linear algebra over C(x) using the cyclic-vector / Wronskian representation. 'Normalising' means raising exponents until the space is one-dimensional, the germ of Riemann's 'rigidity' discussion. This is the text of Riemann's 1857 Nachlass paper 'Zwei allgemeine Sätze über lineare Differentialgleichungen mit algebraischen Coefficienten' (Werke, 1876, No. XXI).
errors: 'Coefficienten der Functionen b_1, b_2, ..., b_n' should be b_0, b_1, ..., b_{n-1} (index slip, consistent with the equations above).

The notation k y + k_1 y^(1) + ... + k_m y^(m) reuses the superscript notation just used for derivatives. It must denote distinct particular solution systems; a derivative y' would not have exponents ≥ those of y. This is ambiguous notation rather than a mathematical error.

Claim that c_0 depends only on y is stated without proof (it follows via the Wronskian, which is multiplied by det(A) under circuits). The degree bound on the b_j is also only asserted. Both are sketches, not gaps in substance.

Step 4 assumes each leading coefficient is a nontrivial linear form in the free constants. Riemann's later deleted remark on the next page ('auch nur um eine Einheit') shows he was unsure about the exact increment.

results.what: Any system Y with the same monodromy and exponents as y is c_0 Y = Σ b_j y^(j) with polynomial coefficients; c_0 depends only on y and the degrees of b_j are bounded.
results.modern_name: Cyclic vector / Wronskian representation of a monodromy-equivalent (gauge-equivalent) local system; Fuchsian contiguity relations
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1857 (Nachlass, publ. 1876); special case Gauss contiguous relations (1812)

results.what: Characteristic-preserving systems form a finite-dimensional linear space, found by solving linear homogeneous equations; either 1-dimensional (determined up to constant) or (m+1)-dimensional.
results.modern_name: Finite-dimensionality of sections of a Fuchsian connection with bounded exponents; rigidity / counting of accessory parameters

results.what: Killing leading terms of canonical branches raises the exponent sum and removes free constants, normalising the system to one determined up to a constant.
results.modern_name: Exponent shifting / Schlesinger-type elementary transformations; normalisation towards a rigid system

deep.surprise_reason: This page is part of Riemann's known Nachlass paper 'Zwei allgemeine Sätze über lineare Differentialgleichungen mit algebraischen Coefficienten', printed in the 1876 Werke. Its content is well known and attributed to him.

checkable.sympy: x=symbols('x'); y1,y2,Y1,Y2=[Function(s)(x) for s in ['y1','y2','Y1','Y2']]; W=y1*y2.diff(x)-y2*y1.diff(x); b0=(Y1*y2.diff(x)-Y2*y1.diff(x))/W; b1=(y1*Y2-y2*Y1)/W; simplify(b0*y1+b1*y1.diff(x)-Y1)==0 and simplify(b0*y2+b1*y2.diff(x)-Y2)==0
checkable.asserts: Cramer/Wronskian formula (n=2) giving b_j/c_0 so that Y_i = b_0 y_i + b_1 y_i' for both i.

checkable.sympy: a11,a12,a21,a22=symbols('a11 a12 a21 a22'); A=Matrix([[a11,a12],[a21,a22]]); x=symbols('x'); y=Matrix([Function('y1')(x),Function('y2')(x)]); Y=Matrix([Function('Y1')(x),Function('Y2')(x)]); Ay=A*y; AY=A*Y; W=lambda u: u[0]*u[1].diff(x)-u[1]*u[0].diff(x); N=lambda U,u: U[0]*u[1].diff(x)-U[1]*u[0].diff(x); simplify(N(AY,Ay)/W(Ay) - N(Y,y)/W(y))==0
checkable.asserts: The coefficients b_0/c_0 are invariant when y and Y undergo the same constant substitution (A), hence single-valued (rational).

checkable.sympy: a,b,c,x=symbols('a b c x'); F=hyper([a,b],[c],x); simplify(hyperexpand(hyper([a+1,b],[c],x) - F - x/a*diff(F,x)))==0
checkable.asserts: Gauss contiguity, an instance of the theorem: F(a+1,b;c;x) has the same monodromy as F with shifted exponents, and equals F + (x/a) F'.
